tagline: Limestone bluffs and river valleys shape a zigzag across northeastern Iowa.
intro: The Driftless Area Scenic Byway zigzags 144 miles across Allamakee and Winneshiek counties in northeastern Iowa. It is paved, with an optional 14-mile gravel loop. Travel Iowa calls this state byway a “rollercoaster road,” with views of limestone bluffs, wooded valleys and river bottoms shaped by the Mississippi, Yellow and Upper Iowa.

The last glaciers missed this corner of Iowa. In the absence of that ice, streams cut deep channels into the bedrock. The National Park Service describes a landscape of deeply entrenched river valleys, sinkholes, caves and springs.

Earlier transportation had to contend with the same relief. Waukon’s railroad to the Mississippi climbed 600 feet and ran 33 miles between places only about 16 miles apart. It opened in 1877 and was abandoned in the late 1960s after a history of marginal traffic.

On a journey toward Postville, Lansing supplies the river-town chapter and Waukon the inland railroad story. Near Harpers Ferry, Effigy Mounds National Monument preserves animal-shaped earthworks. The road continues among historic stone churches, pioneer cemeteries and cold-water trout streams. Postville brings the journey to the junction of US 18, US 52 and Iowa Highway 51, near the meeting of four counties. The city occupies corners of both Allamakee and Clayton counties.
notice: Limestone bluffs rise above wooded valleys and the winding bottoms of three rivers.

moments.title: Lansing
moments.text: Joseph “Diamond Jo” Reynolds built his first boat in Lansing and named it for the town. His own name went on the Diamond Jo steamship line. The river also supplied work beyond boatbuilding. Lansing’s Commercial Fishing Museum presents the town’s fishing, pearl-button and ice-harvesting industries. Passenger trains once followed the Mississippi’s west bank through Lansing between La Crosse and Dubuque. That service dwindled during the first half of the twentieth century and ended on June 8, 1951. Mount Hosmer, on the north end of town, takes its name from artist Harriet Hosmer, who climbed the peak in 1851.

moments.title: Waukon
moments.text: Waukon and Waukon Junction on the Mississippi are only about 16 miles apart, but their connecting railroad needed 33 miles of track and a 600-foot climb. The Waukon and Mississippi Railroad opened in 1877 as a narrow-gauge line. After acquiring it, the Milwaukee Road widened the track to standard gauge. Traffic remained marginal, and the railroad was abandoned in the late 1960s. Waukon sits at the western edge of the deeply eroded Driftless Area, on a plain underlain by Galena Limestone. The headwaters of Paint Creek’s north branch lie in town; Village Creek’s headwaters are just to the north.

moments.title: Effigy Mounds National Monument
moments.text: Bears and birds take shape in earth at Effigy Mounds National Monument, which preserves more than 200 mounds. Most were built in the first millennium CE, during the later Woodland period. The largest, Great Bear Mound, measures 42 meters from head to tail and rises more than a meter above the original ground. The National Park Service recognizes cultural ties between the monument and present nations, including the Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska and the Ho-Chunk Nation of Wisconsin. The surrounding landscape includes forests, tallgrass prairies, wetlands and rivers.
